purpose: Measured (not assumed) throughput of the paper_full_comparison worker mix on the rented L4, to choose the fastest safe execution configuration.

workload.note: Short proxy for the real blocks; identical workload across all configurations.
workload.caveat: This mixed workload conflated two tasks with opposite scaling behaviour. text_char dominates its gain; image generation contributes none. Per-task calibration below is the one that should be used.

configurations.name: concurrent-6-mps
configurations.verdict: rejected: CUDA MPS is 4% SLOWER than plain concurrency here

configurations.name: compiled-serial
configurations.verdict: rejected: crashes on dyrelu, and a net loss where it does compile

findings.concurrency_requires_single_threaded_wor: PyTorch defaults to one OpenMP thread per core per process. Six workers x eight threads oversubscribes an 8-vCPU host and makes concurrent runs slower than serial. With OMP_NUM_THREADS=MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 the same six workers reach 1.81x aggregate throughput. This is the single change that makes multi-process training pay off on this box.
findings.mps_does_not_help: The Multi-Process Service was expected to help by letting kernels from different processes share SMs instead of time-slicing. Measured at 17.74 vs 18.52 cells/min, i.e. 4% slower: at this model size the bottleneck is host-side kernel launch, not GPU context switching, so MPS only adds indirection.
findings.compile_does_not_pay_off_in_training: torch.compile raised BackendCompilerFailed on Dynamic ReLU-B (Inductor pattern matcher: 'Not all inputs to pattern found in match.kwargs', torch 2.8). For the methods that did compile, warm-up cost 20-27 s against 3-4 s of actual training, and even extrapolated to ITERS=3000 the ~24 s warm-up cancels the ~2x steady-state gain. Compilation remains valuable for the steady-state cost microbenchmark (profile_costs), which is what the paper reports; it is not a training-time optimisation at this scale.
findings.saturation: Throughput is flat from jobs=6 upward, consistent with the 8-vCPU host and a launch-bound workload.
findings.concurrency_is_task_dependent: Process concurrency is not a general speed-up: it pays off exactly when a single process cannot fill the GPU. The character LM gained 3.6x from six workers; image generation, whose per-step work already saturates the same GPU, measured 0.98-0.99x across jobs=1,2,4 - flat within noise. An initial mixed-task calibration hid this, because the character LM's gain dominated the aggregate. The blocks are therefore run with different concurrency: jobs=6 for text_char, jobs=1 for image generation.

text_char.note: Tiny model (batch 64, 16-token window, d=128). Launch-bound: a single process leaves the L4 largely idle, so extra processes fill it.

image_generation.note: Larger per-step work (batch 128, 256-pixel sequence, BF16 autocast). A single process already saturates the L4, so concurrency buys nothing and only adds contention. Measured alone at the real STEPS=500 protocol, on image_gen_mnist.
